entities.name: Alexander Ypsilantis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alexander Ypsilantis (d. January 13, 1807) was a preeminent Phanariote statesman and two-time Prince (Voivode) of Wallachia (1774–1782, 1796–1797) and Prince of Moldavia (1786–1788), whose administrative reforms and diplomatic maneuvering significantly influenced the Danubian Principalities under Ottoman suzerainty. Hailing from a powerful Greek family entrenched in the Ottoman imperial administration, Ypsilantis exemplified the Phanariote elite's complex role: balancing loyalty to the Sublime Porte with efforts to modernize and assert greater autonomy for the territories they governed. His career unfolded during a critical period of intensifying Russian-Ottoman rivalry and nascent Balkan nationalisms, positioning him as a pivotal figure in the political landscape of Southeastern Europe.

During his first rule in Wallachia, Ypsilantis initiated a comprehensive legal reform, codifying laws into the *Nomikon Procheiron* (1780), a significant legal compendium that remained influential for decades. He also focused on fiscal restructuring, attempting to streamline taxation and improve public finances, often clashing with the boyar aristocracy over their traditional privileges. His second reign in Wallachia was marked by increased Ottoman pressure and the volatile political climate following the French Revolution, which saw him navigate intrigues involving French and Russian agents. In Moldavia, his brief tenure from 1786 to 1788 was similarly dedicated to administrative consolidation and the promotion of education, though his efforts were often constrained by the ongoing geopolitical struggles between the Ottoman and Russian empires.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alexander Ypsilantis significantly impacted the legal and administrative structures of Wallachia through his *Nomikon Procheiron* and influenced the cultural development of the Danubian Principalities during a critical transitional period. His career exemplifies the complex Phanariote role in shaping regional governance and identity under Ottoman suzerainty.
